conversation.content:
Hello! I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived.

Today I’ll be using the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—to get a quick snapshot of how things have been for you over the past seven days. It’s just 10 questions, takes only a few minutes, and everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to make sure you feel supported.

Shall we start?

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt pretty hard to do?

*shifts a bit in the chair, eyes downcast*

Honestly... it's been really hard. I mean, I'll occasionally smile when my husband tries to be silly with the baby, but I can't remember the last time I really laughed about anything. Even when my sister sent me those funny memes yesterday, I just... couldn't find it funny. I pretended to laugh so she wouldn't worry, but it felt so forced. Everything just feels so heavy right now, like I'm carrying this weight that won't let up.

*quietly* I used to laugh all the time before...
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

No… that’s not true for me. Maybe once or twice I’ve managed a little chuckle, but mostly I just feel flat. Even when something is obviously funny, it’s like the laughter gets stuck. I *want* to feel light again, but it’s like there’s this fog that won’t lift.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs, voice small*

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself I should be excited about little things—like the baby’s bath time or the walk we sometimes take around the block—but the enjoyment barely shows up. I’ll plan it, think “maybe this will feel good,” and then when it happens it’s just… flat. Even my old favorite show is on tonight and I can’t muster the “yay” I used to feel. Everything feels like one more chore instead of something to look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*eyes well up, voice cracks*

All the time... like yesterday when the baby wouldn't stop crying and I couldn't figure out why. I kept thinking it's because I'm not doing something right, that a good mom would know exactly what her baby needs. 

*wrings hands*

And when I couldn't get him to latch properly during feeding... I just kept thinking he deserves a better mother. Someone who instinctively knows what to do. My husband says I'm too hard on myself, but I can't help it. Every little thing that goes wrong feels like it's my fault somehow. 

*tears slip down cheeks*

Even when the diaper leaked at night, I blamed myself for not checking it sooner. I know it's not rational but...
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods quickly, voice tight*

Yes… most of the day I feel like there’s a motor running in my chest. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly think, *“What if he stops breathing?”* or I’ll imagine him rolling off the changing table even though I’m right there with my hand on him. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, the house is safe—but the thoughts just loop. Sometimes I have to get up at night to check if he’s still breathing, and even when I tell myself it’s silly, the worry keeps churning.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*hands twist in lap, breathing shallow*

Yes... it's like this wave of panic hits me out of nowhere. Yesterday I was just folding laundry while the baby napped, and suddenly my heart started racing and I couldn't catch my breath. I had to sit down because I thought I might pass out.

*nervously glances around*

It happens at night too. I'll be trying to sleep and suddenly feel like something terrible is about to happen, like I need to check on the baby right now or... I don't even know what. My chest gets tight and I feel dizzy. The logical part of my brain knows everything's fine, but my body just... panics. 

*voice drops to whisper*

Sometimes I'm afraid to be alone with him because what if I have one of these episodes and something happens.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods, eyes filling again*

Yes… most days it feels like I’m drowning in small tasks. The baby will be fed and asleep, but there’s a sink of bottles, laundry I haven’t folded, texts I haven’t answered, and I just stare at it all feeling paralysed. I’ll think, *‘I should be able to handle this—other mums do’*, but even adding one more thing, like scheduling a pediatric visit, makes my chest tighten. I end up sitting on the couch scrolling my phone because starting anything feels impossible.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*exhales shakily*

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with *‘what-ifs’* about the baby, or I replay every little mistake I made during the day. It takes me over an hour to fall asleep most nights, and then I wake up at two or three a.m. with this knot of dread in my stomach. Sometimes I just stare at the ceiling until the baby stirs; other nights I creep to the nursery to watch him breathe, telling myself I’m being ridiculous but unable to settle. By morning I feel like I’ve barely slept at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

*voice drops, eyes fixed on the floor*

Pretty much every day… I wake up with this heaviness, like there’s a weight sitting on my chest that never really goes away. Even when the baby smiles at me, it’s like I’m watching it through a fog—I feel the warmth for a second, but then the sadness just settles back in. I keep thinking, *“I should be happy, I have this healthy baby,”* but instead I feel hollow. Sometimes I’ll be holding him and tears just start leaking out, and I can’t even explain why.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, wiping cheeks*

Yeah… at least once or twice a week it just spills over. Yesterday I was making tea and suddenly started sobbing—no real trigger, just this wave of misery. I try to do it quietly so my husband won’t hear, but sometimes he walks in and finds me crying over something stupid like dropping a spoon. I feel silly afterward, but in the moment it’s like the sadness just needs to come out somewhere.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*long, shaky breath*

…Yes. Not a real plan or anything, but the thought has—*flashes* through my mind, especially at three in the morning when I can’t sleep and everything feels hopeless. Like, *“What if I just weren’t here?”* or *“Maybe if I got in the car and drove into nothing…”* It scares me when it happens because I don’t want to leave my baby, but the idea that I could make the pain stop pops in for a second or two before I shove it away.

You have shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy-laughter and enjoyment rarely break through a persistent fog of sadness, and you find yourself crying or feeling hollow most days. Despite your deep love for your baby, you are plagued by worries about his safety, sudden panic, and an exhausting belief that every small mishap is your fault. Sleep brings little rest, as anxious thoughts and a knot of dread keep you awake or propel you into his room to check that he is still breathing. You confided that, in the darkest hours, brief thoughts of escape or no longer being here flicker across your mind, though you do not want to leave your child and these thoughts frighten you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 29, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no ability to laugh, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive anhedonia with no enjoyment even for previously pleasurable activities, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent, intense self-blame for routine infant care issues, indicating this occurs 'all the time</sym>, <sym>"Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness, dizziness) occurring both day and night, matching 'Yes, quite a lot</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," paralysed by routine tasks, and unable to start anything, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to anxious rumination and dread, occurring most nights</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent daily sadness, emotional numbness, and frequent unexplained tears, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying spells 1-2 times per week with sudden, overwhelming sadness that feels uncontrollable, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly confirms suicidal thoughts occur "quite often" (3 a.m. episodes), with vivid imagery and frequency matching the highest option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS responses indicate severe symptom frequency across all domains with a score of 29/30, well above the 14-point threshold for urgent referral. The patient endorses <sym>depressed mood</sym> and <sym>loss of interest</sym> daily, plus <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, and <sym>diminished concentration</sym> consistent with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Significant <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic symptoms</sym> suggest a mixed depression-anxiety presentation. Item 10 score of 3 confirms frequent <sym>passive suicidal thoughts</sym> requiring immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call local mental-health crisis line or attend emergency department if thoughts of self-harm intensify or become active
3. Request referral to specialised <med>perinatal mood disorders</med> programme or therapist trained in CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression
4. Discuss with provider starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>sertraline</med> or other <med>SSRI</med> compatible with breastfeeding; consider short-term anti-anxiety medication if panic persists
5. Plan daily 30-minute support window: enlist partner, family, or friend to hold baby while you rest or walk; break tasks into 10-minute steps to reduce overwhelm
6. Encourage sleep-maximising routine-early bedtime, partner handles first night feed if possible, dim lights for pumping or nappy changes to preserve circadian rhythm
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and treatment response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 29: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient: Postpartum mother; responses obtained during routine screening.

Positive indicators for moderate–severe mood/anxiety disturbance:
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q1, 2, 8, 9)
- Daily guilt/self-blame re parenting competence; rumination (Q3)
- Marked anxiety with somatic tension, intrusive catastrophic worries about infant safety; panic episodes (Q4, 5)
- Overwhelm/executive paralysis with routine tasks (Q6)
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to worry/rumination (Q7)
- Passive suicidal ideation without plan ("what if I just weren’t here") – safety concern (Q10)

Patterns: Symptoms present most days; functional impairment in infant care, household tasks, and rest; no reported manic/hypomanic symptoms or psychosis.

Screening conclusion: High likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; immediate safety assessment and expedited referral to perinatal mental health services recommended.
